content: The Canadian Model of Occupational Performance (CMOP) was developed by the Canadian Association of Occupational Therapists. It describes the dynamic interactions and mutual influences between the dimensions of occupational performance. This model is applied using the accompanying Occupational Performance Process Model, which outlines the therapeutic process from the client’s perspective. The primary model illustrates the relationship between the person, occupation, and environment. Spirituality is considered the fourth dimension and is placed at the center of the model to emphasize its fundamental importance. The current CMOP is the result of 30 years of development in occupational therapy. It was initially inspired by occupational performance frameworks proposed by the American Occupational Therapy Association and Reed and Sanderson. However, the need for a national quality assurance system led to its precursor in 1983, titled Client-Centered Guidelines for the Practice of Occupational Therapy. Subsequent refinements are evident in further guideline statements and the publication Enabling Occupation: A Canadian Occupational Therapy Perspective. The model’s national development is a unique feature, ensuring that CMOP does not reflect the views of any single individual. While some assume the model lacks cultural bias and encourage its adaptation, limited research has been conducted on its efficacy in non-Western societies. Beyond cultural relevance, Kielhofner identifies four characteristics of well-developed models, which CMOP possesses to varying degrees. Client-centered practice, which originated in psychology, forms the foundation of CMOP. It integrates systems approaches, environmental theory, and research into flow by Csikszentmihalyi, providing CMOP with a broad interdisciplinary knowledge base. In CMOP, occupational order is viewed through six perspectives: physical rehabilitative, psycho-emotional, socio-adaptive, neurointegrative, developmental, or environmental. These perspectives relate to the performance areas of self-care, leisure, and productivity. The quality of function is assessed in terms of both performance and satisfaction. Disorder may occur within the dimensions of person, occupation, or environment, or when the momentum of experience is disrupted due to unresolved issues. Interventions aim to improve the interactions between person, occupation, and environment through the process of enablement rather than treatment. Enablement involves working with clients to facilitate autonomy and does not primarily focus on performance components. The Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) is a semi-structured interview tool developed to apply the model and is the only prescribed assessment. While it allows freedom to use other supporting assessments, it also restricts the methods of applying the model. Therapists have praised its client-centered approach, relatively quick administration, role in promoting occupational therapy within multidisciplinary teams, and compatibility with other assessment tools. However, these advantages are often compromised when therapists use COPM without adequate training or knowledge of the model, particularly when the tool is applied without implementing the model. Most research evidence related to CMOP pertains to the assessment tool rather than the model itself. Much of this research has been conducted in institutional settings, with methodologies often demonstrating medium to low levels of credibility. This may be attributed to the involvement of the same therapists who contributed to the model’s formulation. While the model is said to be applicable to all age groups and diagnostic categories, few studies have explored its practical application. In July 2007, the Canadian Association of Occupational Therapists launched Canada’s 8th landmark occupational therapy practice guidelines, titled Enabling Occupation II: Advancing an Occupational Therapy Vision for Health, Well-being, & Justice through Occupation. This publication serves as a companion to Enabling Occupation: An Occupational Therapy Perspective (1997/2002) and reflects the growth and development of the profession’s knowledge in occupation-based, evidence-based, and client-centered practice. Enabling Occupation II advances the core concepts of occupation and enablement and their application in practice with clients, education, and research. Drawing on the experience and research of over 60 authors in Canada, it addresses complex sociocultural issues such as diversity, individualism, collectivism, language, economy, and regulation. Several significant developments are captured in these new guidelines, including a deeper discussion of occupation, clear specification of enablement, the practical characterization of occupation-based enablement, and an emphasis on scholarship, accountability, funding, and workforce planning as leadership strategies. The 2007 publication can be considered the triple model guidelines: The Canadian Model of Occupational Performance was expanded to include the concept of engagement. The Canadian Model of Occupational Performance and Engagement (CMOP-E) portrays an occupational perspective that includes and extends beyond occupational performance. The Canadian Model of Client-Centered Engagement (CMCE) captures the profession’s historical focus on client-centered practice, now linked to the broader concept of enablement. The new Canadian Practice Process Framework (CPPF) outlines eight action points for the process of occupation-based, client-centered enablement. The Canadian Association of Occupational Therapists encourages readers of Enabling Occupation: An Occupational Therapy Perspective (1997/2002) to advance their understanding of occupational therapy by reading the companion document Enabling Occupation II: Advancing an Occupational Therapy Vision for Health, Well-being, & Justice through Occupation. Readers are strongly encouraged to use the CMOP-E in place of the Canadian Model of Occupational Performance (CMOP), the CPPF in place of the Occupational Performance Process Model (OPPM), and to refer to the CMCE to bring client-centered practice to life.
